content: This updated Cochrane Review focuses on the use of hydromorphone for managing cancer pain. Pain is a common and distressing symptom in advanced cancer, affecting up to 90% of patients, and it tends to worsen as the disease progresses. Opioid pharmacotherapy is considered the most effective treatment for cancer pain, and hydromorphone is one of the opioid options available. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of hydromorphone in relieving cancer pain and to assess the frequency and severity of any associated adverse events. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing hydromorphone with placebo, other opioids, or active controls in adults and children with cancer pain. The primary outcomes were pain intensity and pain relief as reported by participants, while secondary outcomes included adverse events, serious adverse events, quality of life, early study withdrawal, and death. A total of eight studies involving 1,283 participants (data available for 1,181 participants) were included. These studies compared hydromorphone with oxycodone (four studies), morphine (three studies), and fentanyl (one study). All participants were adults with cancer pain, with a mean age of 53 to 59 years, and the proportion of male participants ranged from 42% to 67.4%. No studies involving children were identified. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was judged to be high. Hydromorphone vs. Placebo No studies were identified that compared hydromorphone with placebo. Hydromorphone vs. Oxycodone Pain Intensity: There was no clear evidence of a difference in pain intensity between hydromorphone and oxycodone, as measured by a visual analogue scale (VAS). However, the evidence was of very low certainty (3 RCTs, 381 participants). Pain Relief: No studies reported participant-reported pain relief for this comparison. Adverse Events: There was no clear evidence of a difference in the incidence of nausea (RR 1.13, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.73; 3 RCTs, 622 participants), vomiting (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.94; 3 RCTs, 622 participants), dizziness (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.44; 2 RCTs, 441 participants), or constipation (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.19; 622 participants). The evidence for all these outcomes was very uncertain. Quality of Life: No studies reported quality of life outcomes. Hydromorphone vs. Morphine Pain Intensity: There was no clear evidence of a difference in pain intensity between hydromorphone and morphine, as measured by the Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) or VAS. The evidence was of very low certainty (2 RCTs, 433 participants). Pain Relief: There was no clear evidence of a difference in the proportion of participants achieving clinically significant pain relief (defined as a 50% or greater reduction in pain) between hydromorphone and morphine. The evidence was very uncertain (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.18; 1 RCT, 233 participants). Adverse Events: Morphine may reduce constipation compared to hydromorphone after 24 days of treatment, but the evidence was very uncertain (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.17; 1 RCT, 200 participants). There was no clear evidence of a difference in nausea (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.30; 1 RCT, 200 participants), vomiting (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.31; 1 RCT, 200 participants), or dizziness (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.88; 1 RCT, 200 participants). The evidence for these outcomes was very uncertain. Quality of Life: No studies reported quality of life outcomes. Hydromorphone vs. Fentanyl Pain Intensity: There was no clear evidence of a difference in pain intensity between hydromorphone and fentanyl, as measured by a numerical rating scale (NRS) at 60 minutes. The evidence was very uncertain (1 RCT, 82 participants). Pain Relief: No studies reported participant-reported pain relief for this comparison. Adverse Events: No studies reported specific adverse events for this comparison. Quality of Life: No studies reported quality of life outcomes. Authors' Conclusions The evidence regarding the benefits and harms of hydromorphone compared with other analgesics for cancer pain is very uncertain. While some adverse events, such as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and constipation, were reported, there was generally no clear evidence of a difference between hydromorphone and other opioids (morphine, oxycodone, or fentanyl) for these outcomes. There is insufficient evidence to either support or refute the use of hydromorphone for cancer pain compared to other analgesics based on the reported outcomes. Further research with larger sample sizes and more comprehensive data collection is needed to provide more definitive conclusions.
